content.en: Saheli teaching a women's studies course? Saheli of the rallies and protests? Believe it or not - yes! More than two years ago, the curriculum for the post-graduate Women's Studies Course for the Mahatma Gandhi International Hindi University was evolving and a core group responsible for this invited Saheli to be a part of the discussion. It came as a pleasant surprise that besides calling hard-core academicians, women from an activist group were also invited to be a part of the process. So one of us decided to explore what exactly it was all about. That was the beginning of our involvement in these discussions and unfolding of an educating experience.

Teaching an academic course was a novel experience. During the discussions about the scope of the subjects, the complexity which should be achieved, the format of the course and so on, we were slightly out of our depth. After agreeing upon the curriculum, various people were taking responsibilities of designing syllabus for papers to be taught over a two-year period. We had vehemently stated that women's health is an area which should be covered in some detail in this curriculum, and lo and behold, the responsibility of designing the syllabus for a paper landed on our shoulders. That is when we started getting a bit worried about what we were in for!

The Indian Association of Women's Studies (IAWS) has always talked about getting academicians and activists together to discuss issues. In biannual conferences of IAWS this mix of academics and activists is visible. Here also with our work as women's health activists central to our understanding, we tried to achieve a balance in the syllabus between the theoretical understanding of women's health and the role of women's movements in striving for better health status for all women. With our diverse backgrounds and varied professional lives we managed to come up with a syllabus for a paper in the M.A. degree course.

While many teachers associated with the women's studies course all over the country are extremely competent, very few of them specialise in women's health. In fact, very few centres offer health as a special subject. Even while working as women's health activists our experience is that many activists in the women's movement find health a difficult subject to engage with. Like a handful of other women's groups across the country, Saheli has a tradition of working on many health-related issues over the past 20-odd years. To translate our hands-on experiences of fighting legal cases, campaigns, surveys, exhibitions, demonstrations and sit-ins on women's health issues and present them in an academic format was as challenging as it was exciting.

In early 2004 we conducted a workshop in the Saheli office for students from the course who had come from Wardha to Delhi on a study tour. We met the enthusiastic bunch of students for the first time, and to our pleasant surprise, both men and women had enrolled for the course. The young men told us of the opposition they had to face from their families, who felt that a women's studies course was a worthless qualification for a young man! For the women, most of them from conservative backgrounds, doing a post-graduation and staying in a hostel involved challenging the norms within their families.

This workshop was more an out-of-the-classroom experience. It did not talk about the methodology of teaching, or history of the subject but it straight away gave the students an essence of what campaigns on women's health have been all about. How demands made on the basis of information and studies can be translated into public activity and protests, whether these work as strategies to achieve the goals, what different forms of protests can be used in such situations and so on. As the flyover shook and window panes rattled, we tried to share our practical work experiences without too much pontification. Answering piercing questions, and formulating answers to complex queries helped us sharpen our own understanding. We also gave the students an assignment to produce a newsletter on the "population problem". And the wonderfully produced assignment we graded six months later were proof that they had found the session as stimulating as we had!

From late 2004, the co-ordinator of the course, Uma Chakravarti began to persuade us to go to Wardha to teach all or part of the whole paper we had designed earlier. In a way, this was extremely positive feedback for our syllabus, since "Women and Health", from being an optional course had been "promoted" to a compulsory course, apparently because the syllabus effectively laid out how an understanding of the politics of women's health could provide an understanding of other linkages that impact on women's lives. But admittedly, our collective hearts sank at the onerous responsibility. This was not something we could do easily, as the expertise required for designing a syllabus is different from actually teaching the entire course. Ultimately, we agreed and decided to teach a part of the syllabus we had designed. Experts, academicians and activists from other parts of the country filled in and competently handled the rest of the teaching responsibility.

Some of us reached Wardha earlier in the year with much anxiety and trepidation. Part of it was to do with teaching in Hindi, part of it was to do with classroom teaching as a form of instruction which we were expected to adopt in the environs of the University unlike in our office in Delhi! Despite delays and disorganisation resulting in our reaching later than planned, a warm welcome from the students and their willingness to continue classes after formal office hours won our hearts and dissipated the anxiety. In classrooms and in the shade of huge trees, we plunged into teaching- which consisted of raising issues and concerns, providing part of the information, asking students to get more information on the subject, evaluating their ability to synthesise information and come up with answers in response to exercises and helping them in becoming questioning, critical and analytical individuals.

Four of the Sahelis were involved in this teaching experience at different points during the course of two years, it was a unique experience for us for a variety of reasons. Firstly, we were proud of being a part of the group framing a curriculum for the first ever masters level programme in Women's Studies in Hindi. Secondly, for some of us teaching a formal course in a university and giving it just enough tilt so that it does not remain only an academic course taught within the confines of a classroom was a new and enjoyable process. Finally, it was also an experience worth cherishing because it was rewarding to see the faces lighting up as the penny dropped as we moved from one argument to the other in the close interactions. The same students came back the next day and asked for more information, and argued with us. The informal nature of the teaching was more conducive to dialogue and exchange of ideas than having a monologue in the classroom full of students. We think this experience has enriched us as much as it probably has the students of the course!

The fact of the Women's Studies Course at the MG! Hindi University hangs in a balance due to administrative problems. If it were indeed to close down, and the experiment crushed before it has time to blossom, it would be a pity, and a loss to women's studies in India.
